title: Do Agents Know When They Succeed? Calibrating Agent Confidence from Internal Representations
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 8 Sep 2026]
    Title:Do Agents Know When They Succeed? Calibrating Agent Confidence from Internal Representations
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:As agentic systems getting adopted rapidly in safety critical applications, it is vital to measure the confidence associated with the agentic actions. In comparison to the traditional machine learning systems, agentic workflows have complex failure modes with planning, tool invocation and dynamic environment interactions. In this paper, we investigate whether model's internal representations provide stronger signals of eventual task success in multi-turn agentic setups. We introduce two complementary methods: Latent Trajectory Dynamics (LTD), which summarizes changes in residual-stream representations across an an interaction trajectory, and the Action Representation Probe (ARP), which predicts success from representations formed at action decisions. Across three interactive benchmarks (Bash, SQL, Python) and three model families (Qwen14B, Qwen7B, DeepSeek6.7B), our methods consistently outperform surface level generation and sequence-based calibration baselines providing a zero-overhead reliability monitor that requires neither prompt alterations nor multi-sample rollouts.

report.summary: New research shows agents’ internal representations can predict task success better than surface or sequence baselines, offering a zero-overhead confidence monitor for multi-turn workflows.
report.background: Agentic systems are increasingly used in safety-critical settings, but they fail in complex ways that traditional ML models do not: planning errors, wrong tool calls, and dynamic environment interactions. Existing confidence calibration often relies on output-level signals, prompt changes, or costly multi-sample rollouts, which may miss failures that are invisible in generated text. This paper asks whether a model’s internal residual-stream representations provide stronger signals of eventual task success in multi-turn agentic setups. It introduces Latent Trajectory Dynamics and Action Representation Probe, evaluated across Bash, SQL, and Python interactive benchmarks using Qwen14B, Qwen7B, and DeepSeek6.7B. The work sits at the intersection of agent reliability, interpretability, and calibration.
key_points: The paper introduces two methods: Latent Trajectory Dynamics, which summarizes changes in residual-stream representations across an interaction trajectory, and Action Representation Probe, which predicts success from representations formed at action decisions. Both aim to estimate confidence without prompt alterations or multiple rollouts.

Across three interactive benchmarks—Bash, SQL, and Python—and three model families—Qwen14B, Qwen7B, and DeepSeek6.7B—the internal-representation methods consistently outperform surface-level generation and sequence-based calibration baselines.

The approach provides a zero-overhead reliability monitor, meaning it can run alongside an agent without extra sampling or modified prompts. This makes it attractive for real-time deployment where latency and cost matter.

The results suggest agent internal states encode useful signals about planning, tool invocation, and environment interaction success. These signals may be available before the agent’s visible output reveals whether the task will ultimately succeed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this points toward runtime reliability monitors that can flag likely failures before an agent acts or finishes. Developers could integrate probes into agent frameworks to gate high-risk actions, trigger escalation, or ask for clarification, reducing reliance on expensive self-consistency rollouts. Regular users may eventually interact with agents that better know when they are uncertain, improving trust in coding, database, and automation assistants. However, the method is evaluated on specific benchmarks and models, so broader deployment requires validation across domains and adversarial settings. It also raises interpretability and privacy questions, since internal-state monitoring touches model internals rather than just outputs.
report.tools: To follow up, explore TransformerLens and nnsight for residual-stream probing, SAELens for sparse autoencoder interpretability, and Inspect AI for agent evaluations. For interactive benchmarks, see AgentBench, ToolBench, and SWE-bench, while SQL-focused work can use Spider. Hugging Face Transformers hooks can help reproduce LTD and ARP. These tools let developers prototype internal-confidence monitors and compare them with standard calibration baselines.
